extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual standards for judging and conducting reasoning: the roles of particulars, general propositions, syllogisms, induction, and deduction; when to use syllogistic form and how to test inductive inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference is from particulars to particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: All inference is from particulars to particulars; general propositions are registers of such inferences already made, and conclusions are in fact drawn according to these registers rather than directly from the general statement itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The major premiss of a syllogism is a formula summarizing prior inductions; the real logical antecedents are the particular facts from which that general proposition was collected. When evaluating an argument, trace it back to the particular observed cases that originally supported the generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: General propositions as registers/short-hand for inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: General propositions (definitions, axioms, laws of nature) function as abridged statements or short-hand notices of particular assumptions we deem entitled to make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State principles and theorems generally for convenience and economy of memory, but remember they stand for collections of individual instances. Ensure that the recorded generality correctly represents the range of particulars it was meant to summarise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major premiss is a formula, not the real antecedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The major premiss of a syllogism is a formula indicating what inferences were judged warranted by previous experience; it is not itself the real part of the argument proving the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the underlying observed facts (the forgotten particulars) genuinely warrant the general principle asserted by the major; use rules of the syllogism as precautions to ensure the record is read correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogism's function: maintain consistency with prior generalisations
rubrics_metrics.description: One principal function of syllogistic reasoning is to prevent inconsistency between conclusions and prior general directions (whether those were framed by induction or received from authority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge an argument in part by checking consistency: does accepting the conclusion contradict earlier accepted generalities? The syllogistic form helps detect such contradictions, not merely by syntactic contradiction but by exposing inconsistency with premises' intended scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogism is not the full analysis of reasoning — induction is primary
rubrics_metrics.description: Although syllogisms are involved in our reasoning, they do not correctly analyse the whole process; the true logical process (when not mere testimony) is induction from particulars to particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing reasoning, distinguish the inductive basis (experience and observed particulars) from the subsequent syllogistic application; do not confuse formality of the syllogism with the evidential basis that justifies the generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogistic form as a security for correctness of generalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: The syllogistic form furnishes an indispensable collateral security for the correctness of a generalisation: it represents reasoning in a form that can reveal inconclusiveness or insufficiency of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the syllogistic form to re-state and test arguments when there is any doubt about validity; it is a tool for verification rather than the essence of reasoning itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: General propositions necessary for considerable progress in reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: General propositions and general language are necessary to any considerable progress in reasoning because they compress the results of long experience into an immediately available shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer forming and recording general principles from sufficient collections of particulars to enable further reasoning; however, ensure those generalities are well-founded to avoid propagating incorrect inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: hardened maxims from insufficient evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A notable drawback of using general propositions is that inferences originally made on insufficient evidence may become consecrated maxims; once particulars are forgotten, minds may not revise earlier false generalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remain alert to the possibility that a general rule is based on inadequate evidence; periodically re-examine the underlying particulars and be willing to revise maxims when counterinstances are found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting insufficiency via generalisation and reductio
rubrics_metrics.description: Converting a proposed particular inference into a general proposition can expose insufficiency of premises, because the generality will include other cases that may be known counterexamples (reductio ad impossibile).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tempted to infer about a single case from sparse evidence, ask whether the same evidence would warrant a broad generalisation; if that generalisation yields known contradictions, the original inference is suspect. Use examples (e.g., historical rulers) to test general implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer induction then deduction when uncertain
rubrics_metrics.description: When reasoning from known cases to an unknown analogous case, it is often advantageous to first induce a general proposition from the known cases and then apply that generality deductively to the unknown case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This two-step (induction → deduction/syllogism) approach enlarges the set of testable parallel cases and increases the chance of detecting defects in evidence. Apply this method especially when cases are complex or when confidence is low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor premiss asserts resemblance between new and known cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In a syllogism the minor premiss affirms that the new case resembles certain previously known cases in specified respects; the minor therefore corresponds to an indispensable part of the real argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the adequacy of the resemblance asserted by the minor: are the shared attributes those that legitimately function as marks for the inferred attribute? If the resemblance is not directly observable, more elaborate trains of reasoning may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal type of ratiocination: attribute-transfer structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The universal form of reasoning resolves into: certain individuals have an attribute; another individual resembles those in certain attributes; therefore it resembles them in the given attribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess inductive inferences by checking whether the resemblance in the listed attributes legitimately supports transferring the target attribute. This is a question of induction, to be decided by canons/tests of correct inductive practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every inference about unobserved cases is induction followed by deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Any process by which we infer about an unobserved case can be represented as an induction (establishing a general proposition from particulars) followed by a deduction (applying that general proposition to the unobserved case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if practical reasoning skips explicit generalisation, when scientific accuracy is required you should recast the argument into induction + deduction to test validity and sufficiency of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trains of reasoning exist when resemblance is not directly observable
rubrics_metrics.description: Trains of reasoning and deductive (ratiocinative) sciences exist to extend inductions to cases where the mark to be relied upon is not directly observable; they are necessary when the minor's resemblance cannot be ascertained by simple observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise when simple single-step inference is insufficient because the minor premise involves non-observable marks; in such cases construct multi-step inferences (trains) to connect observed data to the unobserved target attribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of general language for economy and retention
rubrics_metrics.description: One ulterior use of syllogism and general propositions is cognitive economy: a single careful induction may be recorded as a general proposition so particulars can be dismissed from memory while their practical knowledge is preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating general rules for future application, ensure they accurately summarise the evidence; weigh the convenience of compressing particulars against the risk of ossifying inadequate generalisations.
